chunks.title: Black eye & lid lacerations
chunks.tldr: Black eye: rule out globe injury, roof fracture (subconj haemorrhage with no posterior limit), basal skull fracture ('panda eyes'). Lid margin: align with vertical mattress at grey line/meibomian line → no notch. Canalicular tear → repair within 24 h with stent (3–6 m). Check tetanus.
points: Open swollen lids gently; no pressure on globe until integrity confirmed; CT if needed.
Superficial: 6-0 silk/nylon, out at 5–6 days.
Margin: 5-0 silk vertical mattress 2 mm from edge, tarsus 5-0 absorbable, tie margin so it puckers, skin 6-0/7-0; keep knots away from cornea.
Mild loss → lateral cantholysis; big loss → reconstruction.
Canaliculus: Crawford (bicanalicular) or Mini Monoka.
Tetanus: unimmunised → 250 U immunoglobulin IM; booster if >10 yrs.
Suspected FB in lid → CT; orbital cellulitis risk.
chunks.hook: Panda eyes = base of skull. Subconj blood with no back edge = roof.

cards.q: What does a subconjunctival haemorrhage with no visible posterior limit suggest after trauma?
cards.a: Orbital roof (or other orbital wall) fracture.

cards.q: Time frame for canalicular laceration repair?
cards.a: Within 24 hours (stent left 3–6 months).

chunks.title: Orbital floor blow-out fracture
chunks.tldr: Fist/ball (>5 cm) → floor breaks over infraorbital canal. Infraorbital numbness, diplopia in up + down gaze (IR/IO tethering, positive forced duction), enophthalmos, emphysema. CT coronal. Don't blow nose, oral antibiotics. Repair within 2 weeks if entrapment, >2 mm enophthalmos, >½ floor, persistent primary-gaze diplopia.
points: Diplopia causes: oedema/haemorrhage (settles), entrapment (forced duction +), muscle injury (forced duction −, recovers ~2 m).
Enophthalmos appears as swelling settles.
Check globe: hyphaema, angle recession, dialysis.
Hess chart to monitor.
Small cracks/no herniation/improving → observe.
'White-eyed' blow-out (<18 yrs): trapdoor, little bruising, nausea/vomiting, oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia) → urgent repair.
Repair: transconjunctival/subciliary, free tissue, implant.
chunks.hook: Kid + quiet eye + vomiting + can't look up = white-eyed blow-out → operate today.

cards.q: What is a 'white-eyed' blow-out fracture?
cards.a: Trapdoor floor fracture in a young patient with muscle incarceration, minimal external signs, nausea/bradycardia – needs urgent repair.

cards.q: Sensory sign of orbital floor fracture?
cards.a: Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia (cheek, upper lip, upper teeth).

chunks.title: Other orbital fractures & retrobulbar haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: Roof: kids, upper lid haematoma spreading, globe pulsation, CSF leak. Medial wall: emphysema on nose-blowing, ± MR entrapment. Lateral: big facial trauma. Retrobulbar haemorrhage (orbital compartment syndrome): tight proptosis, ↑IOP, RAPD → immediate lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis.
points: Causes of orbital haemorrhage: trauma, peri/retrobulbar block, vascular lesions, coagulopathy.
Canthotomy: clamp 60 s, cut 1–2 cm at lateral canthus.
Cantholysis: cut inferior crus (scissors parallel to rim, away from globe); canthotomy alone rarely enough.
Superior crus only if still tight (risk to lacrimal gland/levator).
chunks.hook: Rock-hard proptosis + losing vision = cut the canthus now.

cards.q: Emergency treatment for orbital compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis.

chunks.title: Terminology & imaging
chunks.tldr: Closed (contusion, lamellar laceration) vs open (rupture = blunt, weakest point; laceration = sharp). Penetrating = entry only; perforating = entry + exit. Imaging: CT best for IOFB; US gently; no MRI if ferrous FB.
points: Plain X-ray: FB moving with gaze = intraocular.
MRI better for soft tissue/occult rupture but contraindicated with metal.
ERG for retained FB effects.

cards.q: Difference between penetrating and perforating injury?
cards.a: Penetrating has an entry wound only; perforating has entry and exit wounds.

cards.q: Best imaging for intraocular metallic FB?
cards.a: CT (thin axial + coronal).

chunks.title: Blunt trauma: front of eye
chunks.tldr: Abrasion, corneal oedema. Hyphaema (iris root/ciliary body bleed) → watch IOP (corneal blood staining; sickle!). Vossius ring, sphincter tears, traumatic mydriasis, iridodialysis (D-pupil, diplopia/glare). Angle recession → 6–9% late glaucoma. Low IOP with hyphaema → occult rupture.
points: Descemet tears from birth trauma are vertical (vs Haab striae horizontal).
Lens: rosette (flower) PSC cataract, subluxation (phakodonesis, deep AC), dislocation (check pseudoexfoliation, Marfan).
Traumatic aniridia possible in pseudophakes (iris expelled through wound).
chunks.hook: Flower in the lens = punch to the eye.

cards.q: Characteristic cataract after blunt trauma?
cards.a: Rosette (flower-shaped) posterior subcapsular opacity.

cards.q: Risk of glaucoma after angle recession?
cards.a: About 6–9% (late).

chunks.title: Globe rupture
chunks.tldr: Ruptures at weak points: near Schlemm canal, behind rectus insertions, old surgical wounds. Occult posterior rupture: deep AC, low IOP, bullous chemosis/360° subconj blood, poor vision. Prognosis bad if PL or worse. Shield, no pressure, CT, theatre.
points: Prolapse of iris, lens, ciliary body, vitreous.
Asymmetric AC depth is a clue.
Gentle B-scan or CT/MRI to find it.
chunks.hook: Soft eye + deep chamber after blunt trauma = hidden hole in the back.

cards.q: Signs of occult posterior scleral rupture?
cards.a: Low IOP, abnormally deep anterior chamber, extensive subconjunctival haemorrhage/chemosis, poor vision.

chunks.title: Blunt trauma: back of eye
chunks.tldr: Commotio retinae (grey retina, cherry-red spot; clears ~6 wks). Choroidal rupture: crescent concentric to disc; late CNV. Dialysis (superonasal/inferotemporal, young male, slow RD months later). Trauma = ~10% of RDs, commonest in kids. Macular hole.
points: Severe commotio → pigment degeneration, hole.
Direct rupture anterior parallel to ora; indirect opposite impact.
Dialysis may show 'bucket-handle' vitreous base avulsion.
Equatorial breaks at impact site; giant tears.
chunks.hook: White crescent around the disc = old choroidal rupture → watch for CNV.

cards.q: Shape and orientation of an indirect choroidal rupture?
cards.a: Crescentic, concentric with the optic disc.

cards.q: Typical locations of traumatic retinal dialysis?
cards.a: Superonasal and inferotemporal.

chunks.title: Traumatic optic neuropathy & avulsion
chunks.tldr: Sudden loss after head/orbit trauma with RAPD but normal disc (pallor weeks later). Indirect >> direct. Up to 50% improve spontaneously (not if NPL). Steroids controversial (CRASH ↑ death); decompression unproven. Exclude orbital haemorrhage. Avulsion: hole where disc should be; no treatment.
points: Occurs in up to 5% of facial fractures.
Mechanisms: shearing at canal, contusion, haematoma, bone fragment.
CT for canal fracture; MRI for haematoma.
Canal fracture = poor prognosis.
chunks.hook: RAPD + normal-looking eye after a head knock = traumatic optic neuropathy.

cards.q: Why are high-dose steroids for traumatic optic neuropathy controversial?
cards.a: No proven benefit; CRASH trial showed higher mortality with steroids in head injury.

chunks.title: Abusive head trauma (shaken baby)
chunks.tldr: Under 2 yrs; mortality >25%. Multilayered retinal haemorrhages to the periphery (bilateral usually), subdural haemorrhage, rib/long-bone fractures. Presents vague (irritable, vomiting). Examine with a specialist paediatrician; document carefully.
points: Rotational acceleration–deceleration; brainstem injury → apnoea → hypoxia.
Retinal haemorrhages pre-, intra-, subretinal; macular schisis.
Visual loss ~20%, mostly cortical.
chunks.hook: Haemorrhages too many, too deep, too far out = abuse until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Most common ocular sign of abusive head trauma?
cards.a: Multilayered retinal haemorrhages extending to the periphery.

chunks.title: Penetrating injury repair
chunks.tldr: Shield, no pressure, tetanus, systemic antibiotics (± intravitreal), CT, theatre. Signs: peaked pupil, shallow AC, Seidel +. Cornea 10-0 nylon; limbus 9-0; sclera 8-0 nylon/7-0 absorbable. Reposit viable uvea, cut vitreous flush. Primary enucleation only if unrepairable; secondary within 10–14 days (sympathetic ophthalmia).
points: Males 3×, age 15–34; eye protection prevents most.
Small self-sealing corneal wound: bandage CL.
Lens damaged: suture then remove lens; primary IOL often fine.
Vitreous incarceration → fibrous ingrowth → tractional RD.
Posterior lacerations: close sclera first, retina later.
Small lid wound + hammering → lift the lid, look for scleral entry.

cards.q: Suture for corneal laceration repair?
cards.a: 10-0 nylon.

cards.q: Recommended timing for enucleation to reduce sympathetic ophthalmia risk?
cards.a: Within 10–14 days of injury.

chunks.title: Superficial foreign bodies
chunks.tldr: Linear vertical corneal abrasions → evert upper lid (subtarsal FB). Corneal FB: remove with 25G needle at slit lamp; rust ring with burr; antibiotic ointment. Always consider an IOFB (hammering!).
points: Infiltrate, discharge or bad uveitis → treat as bacterial keratitis.
Organic/stone FB riskier for infection than metal.
Cycloplegic/NSAID for comfort.
chunks.hook: Scratches like rain on the cornea → flip the lid.

cards.q: Linear vertical corneal abrasions suggest?
cards.a: Subtarsal foreign body – evert the upper lid.

chunks.title: IOFB, siderosis & chalcosis
chunks.tldr: CT to find (no MRI). Remove: magnet via sclerotomy or vitrectomy + forceps. Siderosis (iron): rusty iris (heterochromia), anterior capsular brown dots, pigmentary retinopathy, progressive ERG b-wave loss. Copper: pure → violent endophthalmitis; alloy → chalcosis (KF ring, sunflower cataract, golden retinal plaques).
points: Inert: glass, plastic, gold, silver.
Stone/organic FBs → high infection rate; give intravitreal antibiotics.
Siderosis can cause glaucoma; retinal damage severe.
Copper less retinotoxic than iron → vision may be kept.
chunks.hook: Iron rusts the eye; copper paints it like Wilson.

cards.q: ERG finding in ocular siderosis?
cards.a: Progressive reduction of the b-wave.

cards.q: Signs of chalcosis?
cards.a: Kayser–Fleischer ring, sunflower cataract, golden retinal plaques.

chunks.title: Post-traumatic endophthalmitis
chunks.tldr: ~1 in 10 penetrating injuries with retained FB. Risks: delayed repair, retained IOFB, ruptured lens, dirty/rural wound. Bugs: Staph & Bacillus (~90%) — Bacillus is fulminant. Prophylaxis: oral moxifloxacin/ciprofloxacin, intravitreal (vancomycin) for high-risk, remove IOFB promptly, culture the FB.
points: Manage established cases like acute postoperative endophthalmitis (tap + inject).
Don't tape the removed FB into the notes — send for culture!

cards.q: Organisms in most culture-positive post-traumatic endophthalmitis?
cards.a: Staphylococcus and Bacillus species.

chunks.title: Chemical injury: emergency
chunks.tldr: Irrigate immediately — tap water if that's all there is; topical anaesthetic + speculum; saline/Ringer's 15–30 min until pH neutral. Double-evert upper lid, remove particles, debride necrotic epithelium. Alkali (ammonia, NaOH, lime) penetrate deeper; acids coagulate (except hydrofluoric).
points: Alkali burns 2× commoner than acid.
Speed + efficacy of irrigation = biggest prognostic factor.
Damage: limbal stem cell loss → conjunctivalisation, persistent epithelial defects, melts; stroma opacity; AC → iris/lens; ciliary body → ↓ascorbate, hypotony, phthisis.
Admit grades 3–4.

cards.q: Most important first step in chemical eye injury?
cards.a: Immediate copious irrigation until pH is neutral.

cards.q: Why are alkali burns worse than most acid burns?
cards.a: Alkalis saponify cell membranes and penetrate deeply; acids coagulate surface proteins forming a barrier.

chunks.title: Chemical injury: grading & treatment
chunks.tldr: Roper-Hall: 1 clear cornea, no ischaemia; 2 hazy, iris seen, <⅓ limbal ischaemia; 3 total epithelial loss, iris hidden, ⅓–½; 4 opaque, >½. Rx: PF antibiotics, steroids for 7–10 days only (then NSAID), cycloplegia, ascorbate, citrate, doxycycline, glass-rod symblepharon lysis, oral acetazolamide. Surgery: amniotic membrane, Tenon advancement, limbal stem cell graft; keratoplasty after ≥6 months; KPro.
points: Steroids beyond 10 days impair collagen repair → melt risk.
Topical ascorbate 10% 2-hourly + oral vit C 1–2 g QDS (not in renal disease).
Citrate 10% 2-hourly + oral: blocks neutrophils/collagenase.
Tetracycline/doxycycline, acetylcysteine = anticollagenase.
Late: symblepharon division, mucous membrane grafts, entropion repair.
Thermal burns: mostly lids; antibiotics; lid surgery; keratoplasty for scars.
chunks.hook: Roper-Hall: count the limbus — 0, <⅓, ⅓–½, >½. Steroids stop at day 10.

cards.q: Roper-Hall grade 3 chemical injury?
cards.a: Total epithelial loss, stromal haze obscuring iris detail, ⅓–½ limbal ischaemia (guarded prognosis).

cards.q: Why taper topical steroids by 10 days after an alkali burn?
cards.a: They inhibit collagen synthesis/keratocytes; sterile ulceration peaks around then.
